title: How are indie developers creating game cutscenes without a full team?
author: Illustrious-Data1712
selftext:
I’ve been working on a small indie game project for a while, and one of the biggest challenges I keep running into is creating story moments that feel cinematic. Building the gameplay itself is already a lot of work, but making proper cutscenes with character animation, camera movement, environments, and atmosphere feels like something that usually requires a dedicated team.

A few years ago, if you wanted a high-quality game trailer or cinematic scene, you probably needed animators, 3D artists, and a lot of time and budget. For solo developers or small teams, it often means cutting ideas because there simply aren’t enough resources to bring everything to life. Recently I started exploring how AI could help with some of these creative bottlenecks.

The way I’ve been doing it so far is combining different tools for different parts of the process. I use ChatGPT for brainstorming story ideas, dialogue, and world-building, image generation tools for character and environment concepts, and Blender plus game engines to build and test the actual scenes. For some cinematic shots and animated sequences, I’ve also been experimenting with PixVerse to see how AI-generated video can fit into my development process.

The biggest challenge I’ve found is not creating one cool-looking clip, but making everything feel like it belongs in the same game. Characters need to stay consistent, the visual style needs to match, and every scene needs to support the story. AI can help generate ideas much faster, but turning those ideas into something that feels cohesive still takes a lot of manual work.

I’m still trying to figure out what makes the most sense for a small team. I don’t expect AI to replace artists or animators, but if it can help me create better story moments and get ideas into the game faster, that’s already valuable. I’d love to hear how other indie devs are handling this. Have you found any tools or workflows that actually help when creating cutscenes?

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
There's plenty of solo animators out there.

First you need to understand how a cutscene is made. In 2d it can be sprites moving around. Not a video file. In 3D it's usually models following animation (what object is where at what time). Both are realtime. And then there's the prerecorded cutscenes that are just video files.

I don't think AI is very good at animation yet, the part where it actually moves objects around. Mixamo is a great help for 3D animation, and so are free animation pack assets.

comments.author: Suspicious_Neck_4069
comments.body: Yes, it’s a lot of work for a solo developer. When I work on a narrative game, I usually create one or two cutscenes first to get an accurate estimate of the time required per scene, which can range from a few hours to a few days. Once you have the script ready, you just need to calculate the time needed and plan your schedule accordingly. Personally, for a "realistic" 3D game, with 80 short cutscenes featuring automatic lip-sync (SALSA), 20 voice-over from fewer, and little or no action in each scene, it takes me five months of full-time work.

comments.author: Acceptable_Fun7453
comments.body:
For a solo team I’d honestly stop treating every cutscene like a mini movie

Block it out in-engine first with the actual game assets, reuse idle animations wherever possible and only hand-build the shots that really need it. Mixamo animation packs can cover a surprising amount.

AI is probably more useful for previs, dialogue, shot lists, and rough concepts than final animation rn. The biggest time saver is deciding what not to animate

comments.author: Low-Cook-3544
comments.body: Other than hiring another solo animator i'd just explore a tool like magnific spaces with an infinity canvas where you can reference the same characters scene-by-scene if you want to try your hand at directing a cutscene with ai.

comments.author: UnderStrangeStars
comments.body:
I'm not an AI dev, but I still think I can contribute here. Have a strong script -- cutscene animation and sequencing takes a lot of time. When I'm working on one, I do well to knock out \~5 seconds of the scene a day if there's a lot of movement. Having a strong script to stick to helps. If you're vibing / iterating a lot you'll either never finish it or it'll be low quality.

So a lot of upfront preparation. Then understand that it's a normal pace to spend a full work session only getting 3 seconds done.
